Pathology of Blood Vessels
Pathology Lab LE 2 · 05 · Florido A. Atibagos Jr., MD

Lecture at a Glance

A laboratory session on three blood vessel lesions, each taught as a case with gross and microscopic (H&E) findings:

  • Case 1: Atherosclerosis → chronic inflammatory response of the intima. Basic lesion is the atheroma / fibrofatty plaque.
  • Case 2: Dissecting Aneurysm → blood splits the vessel wall, producing a true lumen and a false lumen (“double lumen”).
  • Case 3: Capillary Hemangioma → the most common benign tumor of blood vessels during infancy, compared with cavernous hemangioma and pyogenic granuloma.

Main Framework

CASE 1Atherosclerosis
Endothelial injury → plaque (fibrous cap + necrotic center)
→
CASE 2Dissecting Aneurysm
Wall weakness / intimal tear → blood splits media → false lumen
→
CASE 3Hemangiomas
Benign vascular proliferations: capillary vs cavernous vs pyogenic granuloma

High-Yield Orientation

LesionCase clueKey grossKey microscopic
Atherosclerosis68 M, diabetic + hypertensive, tortuous aorta, LV enlargementFatty streak → fibrous plaque → complicated lesion (ulceration, thrombus)Fibrous cap over a necrotic center (cholesterol crystals, foam cells)
Dissecting aneurysm52 M, Marfan’s, acute stabbing chest pain, death with hypotension and shockTrue lumen + blood-filled false lumenBlood tracking within tunica media, advancing edge of dissection

Most Important Concepts Endothelial cell injury is the cornerstone of the Response-to-Injury Hypothesis.
Foam cells are found in the necrotic center of the plaque.
Intimal tear is the most common initiating event of aortic dissection → “double lumen”.
True aneurysm = intact wall. False aneurysm = not all layers involved.
Capillary hemangioma = thin-walled vessels lined by a single layer of endothelium.

Case 1: Atherosclerosis p. 5

Case A 68-year-old male, known diabetic and hypertensive for 20 years, had follow-up consult.
Chest film revealed tortuous aorta and LV enlargement.

Definition Must Know

  • Atherosclerosis is a disease of the arteries that can be considered as a chronic inflammatory response of the intima of the arteries initiated by exposure of the endothelium to various injuries or conditions.
  • Basic lesion is known as “atheroma” or “fibrofatty plaque”.

Sites Affected Extensively (in descending order) Must Know p. 5

  1. Lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries
  2. Coronary arteries
  3. Popliteal arteries
  4. Descending thoracic aorta
  5. Internal carotid arteries
  6. Vessels of the circle of Willis

Key Terms p. 7, 9

TermLecture definition
Arteriosclerosis“Hardening of the arteries”.
Reflects arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity.
AtherosclerosisArteries are hardened because of deposits of atheroma or fibrofatty plaques.
Atheromas
(atheromatous / lipid plaques)
  • Minute yellow intimal lesions that can impinge and rupture on the vascular lumen causing occlusion
  • Occurs in large elastic arteries (e.g. aorta, carotid, and iliac) or large, medium-sized muscular arteries (e.g. coronary, renal, and popliteal arteries)
Atheroma (structure)Raised focal lesion within the intima composed mainly of cholesterol, covered by a fibrous cap made up of smooth muscle cells, macrophages, and extracellular connective tissue.
ThrombusBlood clots forming within vascular intima, consisting of fibrin with numerous platelets, and lines of Zahn under histopathological slides.
Do Not Confuse Arteriosclerosis = general “hardening of the arteries” (wall thickening + loss of elasticity).
Atherosclerosis = hardening specifically due to atheroma / fibrofatty plaque deposits.

Response-to-Injury Hypothesis Must Know p. 8

Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury due to:

1 · CORNERSTONEEndothelial cell injury
↓
2Accumulation of lipoproteins
↓
3Platelet adhesion
↓
4Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium, migration into the intima, and differentiation into macrophages and foam cells
↓
5Lipid accumulation within macrophages
↓
6Smooth muscle cells (SMC) proliferation and extracellular matrix (ECM) production
Study NoteNumbering follows the lecture’s listed order of the contributing events.

Gross: Normal vs Pathologic Aorta p. 6

Normal aorta (left)Pathologic aorta (right)
  • Faint, reddish stain from hemoglobin due to RBC lysis (blue arrow)
  • Smooth surface with occasional faint, small, visible, yellow lipid streaks (green arrow)
  • Top: Aorta exhibiting complicated lesions of extensive atheroma deposits
  • Middle: Aorta showing scattered raised nodules on the intima representing fibrofatty plaque
  • Bottom: Aorta showing precursor lesion of fatty streak appearing as flat yellow linear streaks at its intimal surface

Gross: Atheromas and Thrombus p. 7, 9

Development of Atherosclerosis Must Know p. 10–11

IMAGE AFatty streaks
Minute yellow, flat macules
→
IMAGE BMild (to moderate)
Fibrous plaques
→
IMAGE CSevere, diffuse complicated lesions
Ulceration + overlying thrombus
StageLecture description
A · Aorta with fatty streaks
  • Fatty streaks start as minute yellow, flat macules, fusing into elongated lesions
  • Lipid-filled foamy macrophages are present in the lesions
  • They do not cause significant flow disturbance since they are minimally raised
  • Not all fatty streaks become atheromatous plaques
B · Aorta with mild (to moderate) atherosclerosis
  • Composed of fibrous plaques
  • Plaques are patchy, usually involving only a portion of any given arterial wall
C · Aorta with severe, diffuse complicated lesions
  • Presence of extensive ulcerations (open arrow on the left)
  • Lesion with overlying thrombus (closed arrow on the right)
  • These signify severe atherosclerosis
Exam Trap Not all fatty streaks become atheromatous plaques.
Fatty streaks cause no significant flow disturbance because they are only minimally raised.

SpecimenSeverityAppearance
TopmostSevere, diffuse complicated lesionsPresence of extensive ulcerations along with several thick, lipid plaques

Analogous to islands connected to one another, harbored against a brownish background.

Histology: Artery (Cross-Section) p. 13

Key Findings

  • There is narrowing of the arterial lumen which leads to decreased blood flow.
  • Thrombi can be seen in the blood vessels.
  • Necrosis can also be observed in atherosclerosis, which contains debris from dead cells, foam cells, and fibrin.

Principal Components of Atheromatous Plaques Must Know

ComponentMade up of
CellsSmooth muscle cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes (T cells)
Extracellular MatrixCollagen, elastic fibers, proteoglycans
Intracellular and Extracellular LipidsCholesterol clefts
CalcificationsIn later stage plaques

Plaque Architecture: Fibrous Cap vs Necrotic Center Must Know p. 14

Fibrous Cap (Top)Necrotic Center (Middle)
  • Smooth muscles
  • Macrophages
  • Foamy histiocytes or foamy macrophages
  • Lymphocyte
  • Collagen, elastin, proteoglycans
  • Neovascularization
  • The lesion is limited by tunica media
  • Cellular debris
  • Cholesterol crystals
  • Foam cells
  • Calcium
Lab Exercise Point · Necrotic Center p. 31–32 The necrotic center of an atherosclerotic plaque contains foam cells.
Foam cells are dead macrophages that have phagocytosed lipid droplets, giving them their appearance.
They appear at the center of the plaque due to it having the most lipid infiltration, being the core of the plaque.
This is also where the cholesterol plaques are found.
Exam Trap Distractors used in the lab exercise: smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, collagen.
Smooth muscle and collagen belong to the fibrous cap, not the necrotic center.

Complications Leading to Thrombus p. 33–34

PLAQUE CHANGERupture, ulcer, erosion
→
Exposes the bloodstream to highly thrombogenic substances
→
Induces thrombus formation
→
Further occludes the lumen → downstream ischemia
Exam Trap Hemorrhage was the EXCEPT answer: it is not among the complications listed as leading to thrombus formation (ruptures, erosion, ulceration).

Case 2: Dissecting Aneurysm p. 15

Case A 52-year-old male diagnosed to have Marfan’s syndrome complained of acute, stabbing pain on the chest which progressed and increased in intensity one hour prior to admission.
The patient died 2 hours after admission with hypotension and shock.

Aneurysm: Definition Must Know p. 20

  • Localized dilatation located at any portion of the blood vessel.
  • Localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart that may be congenital or acquired.

False Lumen (Aneurysm) Must Know p. 16

  • Created by conditions that cause inherent weakness on the blood vessel wall (e.g., Marfan’s syndrome).
  • Conditions that may cause weakness of the blood vessel wall:
    • Marfan’s syndrome causes inherent weakness on the tunica media of the blood vessel due to fibrillin deficiency.
    • Uncontrolled hypertension
    • Complicated atheromatous plaque
Clinical Cue Marfan’s syndrome → fibrillin deficiency → weak tunica media → dissecting aneurysm.
Sudden stabbing chest pain followed by hypotension and shock fits rupture of the dissection.

Gross Specimens p. 17–20

Histology: Aneurysm p. 21–22

True vs False Lumen Must Know p. 23–24

Image (p. 23)Lecture description
TopAneurysm is starting to dissect.
True aortic lumen: Aortic lumen (top).
BottomAneurysm that is beginning to split the wall of the blood vessel, which is slowly being filled up with blood.
False aortic lumen: Dissection lumen filled with blood (bottom).
FeatureFalseTrue
Lumen (p. 23)Happens when there is a tear in the blood vessel wall, maybe as a result of traumaWall is intact
False aneurysm (p. 24)Created by the aneurysm itself and it is splitting the wall of the blood vessel—

Advancing Edge and Rupture p. 25

  • Advancing edge / leading edge of the dissection
    • Where the blood that filled up the aneurysm is slowly splitting up the walls of the blood vessel
  • Rupture of the dissecting aneurysm / Rupture of aneurysm
    • Often fatal in most cases
    • May lead to hypotension, hypovolemia, and eventually death of a patient
    • One of the most feared complications

Lab Exercise Points p. 35–38

Initiating Event of Aortic Dissection Intimal tear is the most common inciting event in the vast majority of spontaneous dissection.
This will lead to the formation of a “double lumen”.
Exam Trap Distractors: splitting of tunica media, atheromatous plaque eroding the tunica intima, adventitia rupture.
The initiating event is the intimal tear. Splitting of the media follows it.
True vs False Aneurysm True aneurysms have intact walls.
False aneurysms do not involve all layers of the vessel since some of them have been disrupted.
Exam Trap “True aneurysms have intimal tears” and “False aneurysms have intact walls” are both wrong (reversed).

Case 3: Capillary Hemangioma p. 26

Case A 1-year-old male infant presents with a 1.0 cm reddish, bleeding nodule on the forehead.

Gross: Capillary Hemangioma p. 27

Capillary Hemangiomas Must Know

  • The most common benign tumor of the blood vessels during infancy
  • Frequently seen in infancy and childhood
  • Grossly appears as an attached nodule, some call it a birthmark
  • Bleed upon pressure because the nodule is composed of very friable blood vessels or capillaries

In Children

  • Seen in the skin, particularly on the face and scalp
  • Produce flat to elevated, irregular, red-blue masses
  • Red, succulent, soft, fleshy tumors called “Strawberry Tumor”

Histology: Capillary Hemangioma Must Know p. 28

  • Lobular proliferation of closely-packed, thin-walled, blood-filled capillaries with scant cytoplasm
  • Lined by a single layer of endothelial cells
  • May or may not have thrombosis
Lab Exercise Point p. 39–40 Histologically, capillary hemangiomas are described as thin walled vessels lined by a single layer of endothelium with scant stroma.
Rationale: Lobular proliferation of closely-packed, thin-walled, blood-filled capillaries with scant stroma lined by flattened epithelium.
Exam Trap Wrong choices: multiple layers of endothelium, tortuous vascular channels, atypical endothelial cells.
Key words to look for: thin-walled + single layer + scant stroma.
Lecture-Specific Note Slide 28 says “scant cytoplasm” while the lab exercise answer and rationale say “scant stroma”. Know both phrasings.

Histology: Cavernous Hemangioma p. 29

  • Large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma
  • More infiltrative and involve deep structures
  • Sharply defined, unencapsulated

Histology: Pyogenic Granuloma p. 30

  • Range of benign vascular tumors described as reactive proliferative lesions
  • Rapidly growing, fleshy, red, pedunculated lesions
  • Commonly seen on the skin, gingiva, or oral mucosa
  • Bleed easily and often ulcerate
  • Approximately ¼ develops after trauma
  • 1–2 cm within a few weeks

Core Definitions

  • Atherosclerosis: chronic inflammatory response of the intima of the arteries initiated by exposure of the endothelium to various injuries or conditions
    • Basic lesion: “atheroma” or “fibrofatty plaque”
  • Arteriosclerosis: “hardening of the arteries” → wall thickening + loss of elasticity
  • Atheroma: raised focal intimal lesion, mainly cholesterol, covered by a fibrous cap (SMC, macrophages, extracellular connective tissue)
    • Minute yellow intimal lesions that can impinge and rupture on the lumen causing occlusion
  • Thrombus: blood clot of fibrin + numerous platelets → lines of Zahn on histology
  • Aneurysm: localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart, congenital or acquired
  • Capillary hemangioma: most common benign tumor of blood vessels during infancy

Atherosclerosis

Sites (descending order) Must Know

1Lower abdominal aorta + iliac
→
2Coronary
→
3Popliteal
→
4Descending thoracic aorta
→
5Internal carotid
→
6Circle of Willis

Response-to-Injury Hypothesis Must Know

Endothelial cell injury (cornerstone) → lipoprotein accumulation → platelet adhesion → monocyte adhesion, migration into intima, differentiation into macrophages and foam cells → lipid accumulation in macrophages → SMC proliferation + ECM production

Gross Progression

  • Fatty streak: flat yellow macules → elongated lesions
    • Foamy macrophages present, no significant flow disturbance
    • Not all become atheromatous plaques
  • Fibrous plaque (mild to moderate): patchy, raised nodules, “islands” of yellow
  • Complicated lesion (severe): extensive ulcerations + overlying thrombus, diffuse
  • Normal aorta: faint reddish stain (Hb from RBC lysis), smooth surface, occasional faint yellow lipid streaks
Plaque partContents
CellsSMC, macrophages, lymphocytes (T cells)
ECMCollagen, elastic fibers, proteoglycans
LipidsCholesterol clefts
CalcificationsLater stage plaques
Fibrous cap (top)SMC, macrophages, foamy macrophages, lymphocyte, collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, neovascularization
Necrotic center (middle)Limited by tunica media.
Cellular debris, cholesterol crystals, foam cells, calcium.

Histology Anchors

  • Narrowed arterial lumen → decreased blood flow
  • Thrombi may be seen
  • Necrosis: debris from dead cells, foam cells, and fibrin
  • Foam cells = dead macrophages that phagocytosed lipid → in the necrotic center (most lipid infiltration)

Plaque Complication → Thrombus

Rupture / ulcer / erosion → exposes blood to highly thrombogenic substances → thrombus → occludes lumen → downstream ischemia

Exam TrapHemorrhage = the EXCEPT answer.
